subject: Any reason that Optimize may fail when NUTS doesn't?

messages.author: bbb3e72cd6187a0f
messages.subject: Any reason that Optimize may fail when NUTS doesn't?
parts:
Hi,

I have a model which generates (at least seemingly) good samples when running NUTS, but generates very poor estimates (all parameters at boundaries) when using L-BFGS. Are there any known conditions that would make this happen?

The model is a truncated generalised gamma distribution, with uncertain variates (lognormal uncertainty, they are dark matter halo masses, intrinsically between 10^12 and 10^15 ish). At the moment, all uncertainties are the same (though this will have to change in future versions). Other than the masses, there are four parameters:
  • alpha encoding the power-law slope,
  • logHs encodes the (log) cut-off mass
  • beta encodes the steepness of the cutoff.
  • log_mmin encodes the minimum mass.

The 3 first parameters are all highly covariant, which may be causing problems, not sure (I thought NUTS was fairly good at navigating high covariance?). I'm at a bit of a loss as to what information to to post here. Perhaps I'll just go for as much as I think might help (though it might be a bit to wade through).


So the explicit model: (I'm not posting the functions block here for clarity, but it defines the truncated_GGD_log function which calculates the log of the truncated generalised gamma -- for negative values of the shape parameter)


data {
    int<lower=0> N; // number of halos
    vector<lower=0>[N] log_m_meas; // observed mass of halos
    vector<lower=0>[N] err; //uncertainty in halo masses

    // CONTROLS FOR PARAMETER BOUNDS
    real<lower=0> hs_min; //The lower bound of loghs
    real<lower=0,upper=20> hs_max; //Upper bound of loghs
    real<lower=-2,upper=0> alpha_min; //Lower bound of alpha
    real<lower=-2,upper=0> alpha_max; //Upper bound of alpha
    real<lower=0> beta_min; //Lower bound of beta
    real<lower=0> beta_max; //Upper bound of beta
    real<lower=0,upper=20>mtrue_max; // Upper bound of true masses
    real<lower=0> mmin_min;
    real<lower=0> mmin_max;
}

parameters {
    real<lower=beta_min,upper=beta_max> beta;
    real<lower=hs_min,upper=hs_max> logHs;
    real<lower=alpha_min,upper=alpha_max> alpha;
    real<lower=mmin_min,upper=mmin_max> log_mmin;
    vector<lower=log_mmin,upper=mtrue_max>[N] log_mtrue; //True mass estimates
}

transformed parameters {
   real xmin;
   xmin <- pow(10,beta*(log_mmin-logHs));
}

model {
    vector[N] log10y;
    vector[N] x;

    log10y <- log_mtrue-logHs;
    for (i in 1:N) x[i] <- pow(10,beta*log10y[i]);

    //truncated GGD is beta*10^(alpha*log10y)*exp(-x)/(10^logHs*Gamma((alpha+1)/beta,x)
    log10y ~ truncated_GGD(x, logHs,alpha, beta, xmin);
    log_mtrue ~ normal(log_m_meas,err);
}


I want to use about 25,000 halos for my true run, but have tested with fewer, and wouldn't mind running it with more as well.


I produce my mock halos in the following manner:

library(gsl)

dtggd = function(logm,logmmin,logh,a,b){
  # GSL required!
  return = b*10^(a*(logm-logh))*exp(-10^((logm-logh)*b))/(10^logh * gamma_inc((a+1)/b,10^(b*(logmmin-logh))))
}

qtggd = function(logm,logmmin,logh,a,b){
  return = 1 - gamma_inc((a+1)/b,10^(b*(logm-logh)))/gamma_inc((a+1)/b,10^(b*(logmmin-logh)))
}

rtggd = function(N,logmmin,logh,a,b){
  mmax = logh + 2.5/b
 
  logm = seq(logmmin, mmax, 0.0001)
  cdf = qtggd(logm,logmmin,logh,a,b)
 
  icdf = approxfun(cdf, logm)
 
  x = runif(N)
  return = icdf(x)
}

############## GET MOCK DATA ###################################
N = 5000
err = 0.1
logmmin = 12
logh = 14
alpha = -1.8
beta = 0.7
seed = 1111

set.seed(seed)
intrinsic = rtggd(N,logmmin,logh,alpha,beta)
mock.masses = rnorm(N,intrinsic,std)

To be certain, with this, ie. N=5000, I get the following density plot:



Then I run the following to run stan, and also two optimization runs

############## SETUP RSTAN DATA ################################
data = list(N=N,log_m_meas=mock.masses,err=rep(err,N),
            hs_min=12,hs_max=15,alpha_min=-2.0,
            alpha_max=-1.6,beta_min=0.05,beta_max=1.5,
            mtrue_max=16.5,mmin_min=11,mmin_max=13)

init = list(list(logHs=12.1,alpha=-1.95,beta=1.2,log_mmin=11.1,log_mtrue=mock.masses),   # Far away but reasonable masses
            list(logHs=14.9,alpha=-1.61,beta=0.2,log_mmin=12.5),                         # Opposite side, random masses
            list(logHs=13.5,alpha=-1.61,beta=1.2,log_mmin=11.5,log_mtrue=mock.masses),   # Swap alpha/beta relationship
            list(logHs=logh,alpha=alpha,beta=beta,log_mmin=logmmin,log_mtrue=intrinsic)) # Exact answer if perfect sample

opt.init.exact = init[[4]]
opt.init.bad = init[[2]]

model = stan_model(file="model_NO_S.stan")

############# RUN MCMC #########################################
result <- sampling(model, data=data, pars = c('logHs','alpha','beta',"log_mmin"), chains=4,
                   iter=2000, warmup=1000,cores=4,init=init)

opt.res.exact <- optimizing(model,data=data,init=opt.init.exact,as_vector=FALSE)
opt.res.bad <- optimizing(model,data=data,init=opt.init.bad,as_vector=FALSE)


The results look good for the MCMC: In fact, in this particular case it seems that logHs and alpha are reproduced perfectly (as the median) though beta is estimated as 0.83 rather than 0.7 (it makes sense that beta isn't estimated very well, since it mostly comes from the cut-off where there are basically no objects.


In terms of diagnostics, using the amazing shinyStan, I have:

Chain     accept_stat    stepsize    treedepth    n_leapfrog    n_divergent
All ch    0.8142    0.1093    5.4253    81.8334    0.0119
chain1    0.8282    0.1038    5.691     91.5345    0.012
chain2    0.8056    0.1159    5.2375    59.803     0.0095
chain3    0.8056    0.1089    5.3905    85.8465    0.0135
chain4    0.8176    0.1087    5.382     90.1495    0.0125



Everything looks good I think, as far as I understand. The only things perhaps worth mentioning are the correlation plot:


Where chain 2 is obviously worse than the rest -- this is probably because it starts with random masses. Also the large amount of covariance can be seen in the pairs plot:


Finally, the run took a fair while, especially in the warmup -- not sure if that's normal?:

          warmup   sample
chain:1 767.6131 213.1524
chain:2 539.0624 188.2982
chain:3 798.0353 136.3628
chain:4 852.1482 121.8508


So everything seems pretty much fine. BUT, when I check the results of the optimization runs, it returns this:

> opt.res.exact$par[1:4]
$beta
[1] 0.1685809

$logHs
[1] 12

$alpha
[1] -1.999999

$log_mmin
[1] 12.09832

> opt.res.bad$par[1:4]
$beta
[1] 0.05

$logHs
[1] 14.99999

$alpha
[1] -1.6

$log_mmin
[1] 11


I'm not really sure what else would be useful -- it would be nice if the optimization worked so that I could get quick estimates for testing purposes.


Sorry I feel like I've been spamming you guys lately -- thanks very much for all the work you do. I certainly have not been disappointed.


Cheers.

Yes. Any hierarchical model, for instance, will not have
posterior modes (i.e., max a posteriori or penalized
maximum likelihood estimates are not defined). Nor will
a simple model like

parameters {
real<lower=0, upper=1> theta;
}
model {
theta ~ beta(0.5, 0.5)
}

The thing to do is explore the log density. You can do that
with our diagnose mode in all the interfaces. It lets you
plug in parameters and evaluate the log density. Compare ones
near boundaries to ones that you get with NUTS.

I'll leave the physics model to others --- I tried to highlight
the subject to get the attention of people who may be able to help.

- Bob

In terms of the rest of the model... I'm having other issues with it now. I'll explore them a bit more before reporting back so as to not waste anyone's time.

Cheers,
Steven

messages.subject: Re: (dark matter halo model) Re: [stan-users] Any reason that Optimize may fail when NUTS doesn't?
parts:
Sure. You can look at the "EM goes boom" section of
David McKay's info theory book (free online).

An easy way to see it is to plot the density of the
hierarchical model component highly simplified for
two parameters with fixed prior means:

p(sigma, beta1, beta2)

= Cauchy(sigma | 0, 1) / 2 * Normal(beta1 | 0, sigma) * Normal(beta2 | 0, sigma)

and see what happens as all of sigma, beta1, beta2 -> 0 (be sure that
sigma ->0 from above). Or swap in something simpler for the half-Cauchy.

- Bob

> On Aug 4, 2015, at 10:47 PM, Steven and Jeanette Murray <steven.j...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks Bob,
>
> This is a heirarchical model, so that would be why it didn't work with MAP techniques. Is there an intuitive way to understand why this is? Or some reference you can point me to?
>
> In terms of the rest of the model... I'm having other issues with it now. I'll explore them a bit more before reporting back so as to not waste anyone's time.
>
> Cheers,
> Steven

> > Hi,
> >
>
> Thanks for the detailed model dump.
>
> > I have a model which generates (at least seemingly) good samples when running NUTS, but generates very poor estimates (all parameters at boundaries) when using L-BFGS. Are there any known conditions that would make this happen?
>
> Yes. Any hierarchical model, for instance, will not have
> posterior modes (i.e., max a posteriori or penalized
> maximum likelihood estimates are not defined). Nor will
> a simple model like
>
> parameters {
> real<lower=0, upper=1> theta;
> }
> model {
> theta ~ beta(0.5, 0.5)
> }
>
> The thing to do is explore the log density. You can do that
> with our diagnose mode in all the interfaces. It lets you
> plug in parameters and evaluate the log density. Compare ones
> near boundaries to ones that you get with NUTS.
>
> I'll leave the physics model to others --- I tried to highlight
> the subject to get the attention of people who may be able to help.
>
> - Bob
>
> > The model is a truncated generalised gamma distribution, with uncertain variates (lognormal uncertainty, they are dark matter halo masses, intrinsically between 10^12 and 10^15 ish). At the moment, all uncertainties are the same (though this will have to change in future versions). Other than the masses, there are four parameters:
> > • alpha encoding the power-law slope,
> > • logHs encodes the (log) cut-off mass
> > • beta encodes the steepness of the cutoff.
> > • log_mmin encodes the minimum mass.
> > The 3 first parameters are all highly covariant, which may be causing problems, not sure (I thought NUTS was fairly good at navigating high covariance?). I'm at a bit of a loss as to what information to to post here. Perhaps I'll just go for as much as I think might help (though it might be a bit to wade through).
